utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam and good morning to you. So all the accused are here. Defence as last Friday. Prosecution, today there is Ms. Soljan as well present. So no preliminaries, I take it. All right. So we have the next witness. Let him -- let's bring him in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for having invited me to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I didn't invite you. It's the Prosecution that has invited you and you are a Prosecution witness. Before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, which Madam Usher is going to hand to you now. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. So this is not the first time you're testifying before this Tribunal. You've testified before and you had some protective measures. We have also put in place for you some protective measures, namely, you will be testifying under a pseudonym, not with your name and surname, and you will be referred to as Witness 126, if I remember well. You are also going to testify with facial distortion and also voice distortion. In other words, your face will not be shown and your voice will not be transmitted outside this courtroom. I suppose these have already been explained to you. Have they been explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you're satisfied with these arrangements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Ms. Soljan will go first. She will be examining you in chief and then the various Defence teams will follow each other in cross-examining you. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. If I could please have the usher's assistance to provide the witness with what has been marked for identification as P02286, please. Now, Witness, please take a look at this piece of paper and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: -- tell us whether your name is written on it, without saying your name, please. Is your name on there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could please show that paper to my learned friends? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could go into private session for the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Turning your attention specifically to the 11th of July 1995, can you please tell us where you were that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: That morning, I was in my house in Srebrenica, together with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If we could actually go briefly into private session for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Borovcanin? THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that somebody's microphone is on because we are not receiving the witness's voice. We are receiving interpretation but not the witness's words. We can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I checked the last time we had someone testifying with voice distortion. That was indeed the case because I checked to see on all the channels whether you could hear the testimony. Sit down -- you could hear the testimony and it could not be heard. On that occasion, I can confirm but I don't know what the arrangement is. I think inside the courtroom, they should be able to hear. It has got nothing to do with the microphones on or not on because I have been using eagle's eyes to make sure that there are no microphones switched on while the witness is speaking. Were the others getting her testimony? So it could well be that he was not on the right channel? General Miletic, were you? You were sitting next to him. Were you receiving the testimony or not? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] No, no, not in my earphones. I could hear the voice in the courtroom but not through the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's get the witness to say something now. I'm going to switch off my microphone. Madam, please do say something. Just say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What am I supposed to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all. We just wanted to make sure that what you are saying is being heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. [Microphone not activated] If that happens again, please, let us know straight away as Mr. Borovcanin did. Thank you. All right. Sorry for that interruption. Ms. Soljan, please go ahead. We are in private session by the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Madam, you have stated that on the 11th of July 1995, you were at your house in Srebrenica. What was happening --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: -- this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: That morning, early, when I got up, I saw people moving in large numbers towards Potocari, carrying their belongings, suitcases, bags. They were carrying things and helping each other. And I and my brother were watching this, and my brother says, "What are we going to do, sister? Are we going to go and join them as well?" And I said I was not too keen because I thought that Srebrenica was not supposed to fall. It was a protected area, demilitarised area. It wouldn't fall. These same people would go back and we exchanged views and opinions for a while, and it was almost 11.00 on that morning. The people had already left, most of them left Srebrenica. I heard a woman screaming, "My son. You got killed. And I did not even get a chance to bury you." It was around 11.00. I did not have a watch but I believe it was around 11.00, when I got out of the house and all over Bojna I could see the Serb soldiers approaching, and I could see some people hiding and I could hear shots and the noise of fire all around my fence. And even before Srebrenica fell, there was shelling for days, and even after Srebrenica fell, the shells never stopped falling around Srebrenica and in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, why were these people leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Because they realised that we would all be killed. They saw people being killed. They could hear fire and the DutchBat members kept telling them to go to Potocari. And people were moving together with the DutchBat soldiers. And after them, I saw the Serb soldiers and all over Bojna I could see armed people and I'm sure that those were Serb soldiers approaching the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: My brother and I got ready and started slowly moving towards Potocari. We saw that almost everybody had left Srebrenica. There were a few people left, however, who were either disabled or elderly, who didn't know what was going on. The Serb soldiers had already entered Srebrenica and captured them. In any case, whoever remained in Srebrenica did not survive, did never come to Potocari and was never seen again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Witness, around what time did you and your brother arrive in Potocari? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: We left around 11.00, and we moved slowly. There was constant shelling. There were the dead people and blood along the road, and there were a lot of people screaming for help. There were those covered in blood and dead and not moving. However, nobody looked at others. Everybody minded their own business. They wanted to get to Potocari as soon as possible, to save themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you tell around what time you arrived in Potocari? How long did it take you to get to Potocari from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: It may have been about half past 12 or 1.00 in the afternoon. We did not walk all the time. We had to hide from time to time. When we heard that bigger shells would fall, we would hide behind a tree, a house, and when the things subsided, then we would continue walking again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon arriving in Potocari, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: As I arrived in Potocari, together with my brother, there were a lot of people there, thousands of people were there, and people kept on arriving after us, but in smaller numbers. There were a lot of Bosniak people there who had come from Srebrenica. On that day, the Serb soldiers did not come there. We did not see them on the 11th of July or at least I didn't see a Serb soldier. I did not see anybody coming there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you spent the night, the evening of this 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: When we arrived there on that day, there were a lot of people. That's how night fell. It started getting cold and my brother said, there is a shed over there, why don't we bring some straws and there is an old car, a little van, there we will find shelter in that van. That's where we spent the night. We were hungry but it did not occur to us to feel hungry. We had not taken anything with us but it was okay. We did not actually feel hunger.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what happened the next morning, on July 12, when you woke up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: We did not even sleep. We were awake all night. We were awaiting for the dawn to see what would happen. All I wanted was to go back home. However, around 10.00 on the 12th of July, there was panic among people. There was screaming and wailing, and women started shouting, "There come the Chetniks." And they were pointing their fingers at different places. And there is places up there, Pecista, Budak came from there. You could see that they had already started torching. They were not torching valuable and important things, but some unimportant things, and they were wearing camouflage uniforms, olive-drab uniforms and black uniforms. They narrowed the circle around us and they started moving among the people who were there in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you see whether or not they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes. They were all armed. I did not see a single of their men without being armed to their tooth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And Ms. Soljan, if you're going to pursue this item, this matter, with further questions relating to specific individuals, I think we need to go into private session as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There aren't going to be many questions, but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Already, I have my doubts in reality. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd just like to remind you not to mention any names, and if you are about to mention names of people, to let us know so that we can go into private session. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked them for them, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: We are in private session now, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, but you asked her for names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: It's true I asked her if she had recognised any soldiers. The next question was going to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, what happened next? You had mentioned that in the morning of July 20th [sic], you saw soldiers arriving. There was panic. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just correction. It says July 20th in the transcript. It should be July 12th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 11th of July, I left my house, and on the 12th of July, the Serb soldiers came to Potocari. They came to us and were there around us on the 12th, not the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: That morning, we saw -- well, shall I speak about it again, that morning, when we left the house or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, no. I am referring now to the 12th of July, when you already were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: All right, the 12th. Very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, please, before you open your mouth to say something, make sure that Ms. Soljan's microphone, the red light, is off. Don't jump --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You may continue describing the 12th of July, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Should I speak? Who should speak now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if you can -- I asked you if you could tell us what was happening after the soldiers arrived on the 12th of July 1995, into Potocari. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: The soldiers came and they started to walk amongst the people. There were a lot of horses around because people had brought the feeble persons on horses, the soldiers began to ride and play around. They didn't really go deep into the crowd but sort of more on the edges of it. And the men would tell us, "Stop crying, stop creating panic. Stop making all these noises. You are all going to get to the free territory." Some spoke like that. Others said, "Had you not done what you did in 1992, we wouldn't be having a war now." They said, "Look at Srebrenica, you will never go back there again. Look, turn back and look." That's what they said. Then they said, "Don't think that we are not going to find you in Tuzla and Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, where did you and your brother go once the soldiers arrived into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: My brother and I were there. My brother was still under the truck. And I would go outside to see what was happening, could we go out, should we leave, should we return home. We were still very indecisive. We didn't know what would happen. If I heard something, I would go and see him and tell him, I told him don't worry about anything. They say that we will all be transferred safely to Tuzla or Sarajevo. In any case there won't be any problems and then I encouraged him a little bit. I didn't speak to him about bad things. I wanted to encourage him so that he could reach the buses. They were telling us that there would be buses and trucks arriving to transport us. Then on one occasion, I left for a walk, a little bit farther off and I could see that buses really did indeed start arriving and there were trucks, and I told him, "Let's go closer. Let's not wait and be the last ones. Let's go down there slowly. Let's go to the buses. The other people are going to." So we started to get closer. I also saw -- I was happy to see the people that I recognised. I believed that they are going to give some sort of help. I didn't believe that what happened would happen. I thought something better would happen, but actually the worst possible thing happened in Potocari. We all know. It's all clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, please, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could perhaps have a break for the witness now, before the cross-examination begins? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all right with the Defence teams? We need to have a 30-minute break because of the redactions and we will have the break start from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is going first? Ms. Condon? Ms. Condon is appearing for accused Popovic, Colonel Popovic, in this case, and she will be cross-examining you first.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I pre-empted the matter. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it please the Trial Chamber, we have no questions for this witness also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Meek was representing Colonel Beara. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good, Your Honours, we don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was for accused Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Mr. Lazarevic is appearing for accused Borovcanin in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We should move to private session very early just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, but I also noticed that you did not switch off your microphone, when the witness was talking. Make sure that you switch it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. So now it's even more important, Madam, to allow a pause between question and answer, which you haven't been doing in spite of my exhortation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now we are talking about the situation in Potocari. It was a very large crowd of people there. There was a lot of commotion going on and all those people wanted to get to the buses. Is that a true picture of the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: What the people wanted to do most was to return home to -- return to their homes, but when the chaos ensued and the men began to be separated from the women, then the people tried to get close to the buses, to the trucks, to be transported out. But no truck with the men crossed into the free territory of the federation. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony today, you mentioned a human chain consisting of Serb and Dutch soldiers who were holding hands and preventing more or less the entire group of refugees to push towards the transport. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well. That's how it was. They were holding hands. A Serb soldier and a Dutch soldier and then they would raise their hands, let through however they wanted, how many people they wanted to, and when they felt that the bus was full, they would then lower their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A few more questions about this. Can you please tell me whether this human chain was long? How many people could have been in that human chain, both the Serb and the Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: I couldn't really give you the number. There were many Serb soldiers, it's true, many more than Dutch soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So the chain mostly consisted of Serb soldiers who were holding back the crowd of refugees and with the odd Dutch soldier holding hands with them, is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: I wanted to say that on the road, when they were letting people pass through to the buses, there was one Dutch and one Serb soldier, but in Potocari, there was a big mass, a large number of Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you help me to understand your answer so that it is completely clear? I'm not doubting that there were many more Serb than Dutch soldiers in Potocari. What I'm interested in, though, is just the chain, when they were holding hands. Were there more Serbs there or Dutch or was it one and then the other? Did they alternate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- they were alternating.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is next? Mr. Krgovic who is appearing for General Gvero, will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that we have some problem with interpretation because the transcript here reads on page 40, line 8, the answer was "they were alternating." And the way I understood the witness said there was one Serb soldier, then next to him a Dutch soldier and then again Serb soldier. That's the way, one on one, that's -- okay. Okay, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I heard you. I don't think there is a problem but let's move to Mr. Krgovic's cross-examination. And again, Mr. Krgovic and Madam witness, please allow for a short pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Madam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a few questions to you about your stay in Srebrenica shortly before you left for Potocari.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When I put the question to you, can you please make a short pause before answering so that we do not overlap and in that way, reveal your identity? We are speaking the same language. We understand each other. And it's possible then to overlap and I'm telling you this both for the sake of the interpreting and also so that we do not reveal your identity. So when I give you a sign, then you can begin to answer. Is that all right? Madam, that day, you said, responding to the Prosecutor's question, that you left your house at around 11.00 and went out into the street in Srebrenica; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That day, in the morning, between 10.00 and 11.00, until you left Srebrenica, Srebrenica was not shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: No, it's not correct that it wasn't shelled. It was shelled. The whole time, five days before that, when they began, they never stopped. That night, the shelling never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about that morning, that morning, between 10.00 and 11.00, right until you left for Potocari, Srebrenica was not shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: It was always shelled. It's not true that it wasn't shelled. They didn't stop shelling. You could hear the shells non-stop in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am interested specifically in the town of Srebrenica, in the area where you were, and this particular period. I'm asking you about that. I'm going to put some questions to you later about the other time. So that morning, between 10.00 and 11.00, until you left Srebrenica, Srebrenica was not shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Srebrenica was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this period that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes, this period. It was shelled the whole time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. Sustained. Next line of questions, please, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm talking about the 10th of July. On the 10th of July, between 8.00 and 9.00 in the evening, Srebrenica was not shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: No. It is not correct. Srebrenica was shelled from five days before that. And when it began, there were non-stop shells. I would like to recall that image for you, if I could, and to say how many people were killed five days before Srebrenica fell. On the 11th of July, the electricity was cut off, the water was cut off, the different small wells and streams that existed where people stood in line, the whole time, about 50 people on average would wait there to fill a canister with water, then when the shell fell, five, 10, 20 dead people would be left, even more. This is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, on the 10th of July at 3.00 p.m. onwards, until, let's say, 5 p.m., Srebrenica was not shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. What is correct is that it was shelled non-stop, that it did not cease. I wasn't paying attention with a stopwatch when the shelling was going on or not, but you had to keep on the run the entire time and you could hear shells in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, in Srebrenica, on the 10th and 11th of July, no building was hit during that period when you were there. I'm talking about the centre of Srebrenica town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Shells were falling. I didn't go from building to building to see where the shell hit and where it did not. You could hear the shelling, there was shooting, people were screaming out. There wasn't a single day when people were not driven to the medical centre because of shell wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, did you personally see in Srebrenica, in that period, on the 10th and 11th of July, that a house was hit or that anybody was killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: I was at my house. I was going about my business. I didn't go around to see when and if people were killed. You could just constantly hear shelling. First of all, for a while, it was quiet, and very nice. There was no food in Srebrenica, but mostly there was no shelling. But then before the fall of Srebrenica, some 15 days before that, the shells started to fall and then this became more intense and then even more intense and then one or two nights before the fall, it never stopped. The shells kept raining down. You could hear the noise; it was pretty loud. They were firing from all weapons. This is definitely what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. You personally did not see a single shell fall in Srebrenica or any casualties because of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: Yes. I did see it. At a water source near my house. That's where I saw a shell fall and I saw that three women were hit. They were killed. And there were other people hit by shrapnel and wounded and they were taken off to the Srebrenica medical centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was objecting to the repeated question about seeing the buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But any way, it was useful to wait because she gave the answer in any case. Yes, Mr. Krgovic. Wait one moment, Mr. Krgovic. Madam, I appeal for your cooperation a little bit. I am informed by the interpreters that they are encountering some difficulties in trying to follow your testimony and translate it into both English and French. There are two reasons for this. One reason is that you're speaking too fast and you need to slow down a little bit. The other reason is that you are speaking too much close to the microphone and you're also speaking very loud and that is not very good for the interpreters. So if you could distance yourself a little bit from the microphone and lower a little bit your voice, then the interpreters will be much happier. All right? Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, what you were talking about earlier was not on the 10th and the 11th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: It was on the 10th and the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now it's over, Mr. Krgovic, no more questions on whether it was the 10th or the 11th and whether she has seen this. Move to something different because you've been labouring on -- labouring this a little bit too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just going to put my final question. And the reason why I put these detailed questions is precisely because I would like to show the witness a document relating to the specific time period and the shelling that I was asking the witness about. And that will be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, if I were to tell you that there was a video footage of Srebrenica on the 10th and 11th of July, recorded by people from Srebrenica, Muslims, which do not show what you are testifying about today, would that perhaps induce you to change your position on the shelling of Srebrenica on the 10th and the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question for the time being. Only when I tell you. So does the video that you are referring to span, go over a span of 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The footage covers the period that I asked the witness about, so the date and the time that I asked the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Show her whatever you want to show her but -- yes, Ms. Soljan, one moment before we start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I still think we need a clearer explanation about what particular time period these video clips -- did not last 24 hours, so what particular time period is he talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can deduce that from the questions that he put earlier on, 10 to 11, 3.00 to 6.00 or whatever. But again, I mean, let's see. Let's start the video rolling, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't hear the sound. Maybe we could stop the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem that we have obviously is this. Let's take it, for argument's sake, agree completely with you that this footage -- on this footage, there are no sounds of any shelling. Does that mean that on the 10th and on the 11th, there was no shelling? It only means that during that period, during which the film was being shot, there was no shelling, which does not contradict the witness because the witness told you that she was not timing the shelling and is not in a position to tell you what time of the day or of the night there was shelling. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not the only evidence that Srebrenica was not shelled on that day. Even the Prosecution military expert, Mr. Butler in the Krstic case, established that there was no proof or evidence that Srebrenica was shelled over those two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's just not correct, if he's going to be stating Mr. Butler. That's outrageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think the existence of this video, in juxtapose to what the witness has been testifying is not going to change anything. You have her evidence which says one thing and the video which says another, and if you feel that the version portrayed by the video is supported by other evidence, leave it there. If you insist on showing it to her, we show it to her. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, there is no need to show this footage. I accept your remarks completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at the same time, there is a limit. Yes, further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau? Madam Fauveau is appearing for General Miletic and she will now be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Madam, you said a while ago that members of the DutchBat were together with the Serb military on the road when people were being asked to board the buses. Would you say that the DutchBat members were working together or hand in hand with the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: I don't know if they were cooperating or not or working together. I saw them together and I know that they were Dutch soldiers above Srebrenica protecting the Srebrenica safe zone, and I know that there were Serb soldiers too, but Srebrenica was shelled above the Dutch soldiers, the town itself and its environs were shelled and I know that people were leaving Srebrenica that day because the DutchBat had come from up there and said, "Go in the direction of Potocari." Serb soldiers were walking behind them tightening the circle, and that's how we reached Potocari. A lot of things happened in Potocari. I couldn't follow everything that was going on, but that place that I told you about near the buses, there were one Serb soldier, one Dutch soldier, alternating. They were holding hands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They held hands and then when they would allow enough people to pass for the bus, they would raise their hands and then when they felt enough had gone, they would put their hands down. Then there were other people in the batteries factory, in the maintenance plant. I didn't see each of the factories. I saw that there were a lot of people. I didn't go into the factories but there were thousands of souls there. That is beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we have a problem here controlling the witness. Could you ask the witness to just answer the question and not go beyond the question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Fauveau -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a very broad question and I think that the witness answered the question to the best of her abilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the question was very simply put, whether they were cooperating. And she started off with saying that she didn't quite know whether they were cooperating or not. And the first part of her answer was quite relevant but the rest wasn't. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Madam, when it came to moving towards the buses, did you notice any problems between the DutchBat soldiers and the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-126
utterances.text: I did not notice any problems among them at all. I mean, that they had problems with each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we move into private session because I have a few questions that may help some people to identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, Madam Fauveau has finished her cross-examination here and Defence team for General Pandurevic stated they have no cross-examination for this witness. Is there re-examination, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (redacted

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, thank you so much for having come over to give evidence in this case. Our team will assist you to facilitate your return back home and on behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for having invited me, and for bearing throughout my testimony, for bearing with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not at all. Thank you. I take it you have the next witness in line, no? Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, exhibits. Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We have P02286, which was the pseudonym sheet under seal. The PIC 00034-1516. This was a aerial map marked by the witness indicating the location of the house today. And then PIC 00035 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objections? Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we will need to redact that, Your Honour, what's just been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree. So let's redact lines 24 and 25 and -- of page 61, and -- well, actually we can redact only line -- from line 25 after the words, "Then PIC 00035" til the next line which is first line on page 62. Thank you for that observation, Mr. Josse. Are there any objections? Okay. So your documents so tendered are being admitted. Any of the Defence teams -- yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to tender Exhibit number 5D96 which is a statement made by the other person, page 2, the last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think this would also need to be kept under seal because -- this is the statement of the other person. Yes, let's see whether there is an objection first. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry for stepping in. Just that I was present at the last trial. We are in private session, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you like this but we were -- yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like simply to inform the Chamber that we will request a correction officially of the transcript concerning page 27, line 15 to 19, since the second answer of the witness does not correspond at all to the first one and we will request from the translation service to compare the transcript to what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for pointing that out. Can we usher in the next witness? That's going to be 92 ter witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's Mr. Vanderpuye's witness. If we could usher him in as well, I hope he's listening but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat? Because I was discussing something with Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is Mr. Vanderpuye's witness and he may be outside as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have the break if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That might be simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can have a 30-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we just need to make a quick modification or, rather, change the exhibit numbers on the two exhibits that were admitted in the previous session. We have the correct numbers for them now. So what had been admitted as PIC 00034-1516 should in fact be PIC 00035 and what had been admitted as PIC 00035 should be PO 2289. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I welcome you to this Tribunal and to this case where you are a Prosecution witness. You are soon going to start giving evidence. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of a solemn declaration that is tantamount to an oath, an undertaking, a solemn one, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. Please read it out and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please take a seat. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the request of the Prosecution, we have granted you some protective measures. These are -- you will be testifying with a pseudonym rather than with your name and surname. And also, public outside this courtroom will not be able to see your face because we have granted facial distortion. Have these been explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And are you satisfied with this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, who is a member of the Prosecution team in this case, will be examining you in chief after presenting some previous statements that you have made. And then I don't know if that will happen today or tomorrow, then you will be cross-examined by the various Defence teams. So Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, gentlemen. Your Honour, I had planned to proceed as I did with another witness and that is to first elicit or qualify the underlying statement, that's proposed to be admitted pursuant to 92 ter, and then to read a summary, and with the Court's permission and hopefully without the objection of counsel, to lead the witness on, I think, a relevant matter relating to these proceedings and, particularly, the execution at which he was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see what the procedure or practice is. If there is an objection to a leading question we will entertain it. If not, you will proceed in the absence of objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness take a look at P02287, if I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask to you take a look at that document, and without telling us what's on it, can you tell us whether you were the person named in that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would Defence counsel like to examine the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall having signed a statement given to the ICTY on or about the 18th of May 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prior to signing the statement, did you have an opportunity to read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the statement that you signed a truthful one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to read your statement prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you read the statement in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the language in which you originally gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What is your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During the course of reviewing your statement, did you indicate that it contained certain errors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were the errors that you indicated as follows: With reference to paragraph 1, to the phrase as time passed, most of the people in my village left and went to the UN safe area, with respect to that reference, should that be placed in the context of the events of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to a reference in paragraph 5 to M53, M53 firearms, should that be a reference to machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the transcript. There is an ambiguity here because it's not clear whether he's saying he's spotted the mistakes in his statement when he reviewed it, having made it in May 2000, or when he reviewed it on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I think you should address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the errors that I'm speaking of now, are those errors that you pointed out yesterday to me in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to paragraph C, there is a reference to persons surrendering who were those who had not crossed the road as we had done. In the context of that statement, is it in fact true that those people who were surrendering were actually ahead of you and not behind you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: No. They were in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so is it the case that you had not in fact crossed the road yet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: That's correct. I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, contextually, the observations that you relate in the statement to the killing of surrendering group in paragraph 7, did that occur after or before your group or you had succeeded in crossing the asphalt road somewhere near Sandici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I should rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt but my learned colleague is referring to paragraph C on page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the interpreters are not hearing what -- cannot hear what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to them. My learned colleague is referring to paragraph C on page 69, line 6, and going through the statement of this witness, I never noticed any paragraph C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: C in the supplement, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be 7, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that clear enough now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Defence counsel were handed over the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now? All right. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic and thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is a reference -- I'm sorry, you asked me to rephrase the question; is that right? I think that's correct. Okay. There is a reference in this statement relating to the killing of a surrendering group, that's mentioned in paragraph 7. That is the group of surrendering people that had crossed the road or were trying to cross the road. Did that occur after or before the witness had crossed that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: It happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The reference in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 is somewhat long, so could you help me find the exact passage in paragraph 7, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment. If you look to the end of the first paragraph in paragraph 7, there is a reference in the last sentence to the persons surrendering who were those who had not crossed the road as we had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And thereafter, the reference that the witness is making are to observations that occurred after that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is also a reference in paragraph 7 to the group proceeding in the direction of Zvornik. And should that be in the direction of Kuslat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, yes, towards Kuslat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And finally there is a reference in paragraph 12 indicating that the military police were stationed at the factory where the witness was held captive. Should that also include the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from these errors, sir, does the statement fairly and accurately reflect your declaration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Maybe just some dates, the last dates, perhaps from the 15th onwards. I would not be able to say precisely, it was such and such a date, because we were so tired and hadn't slept much, hungry. So that a person cannot say specifically and in detail it was such and such a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you have some -- is it fair to say that you have some reservations about the accuracy of the dates that are in this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Can you please explain your question in a little more detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are the dates that are in the statement exact? Or are they approximate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: They are approximate. They are not 100 per cent exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from the approximation of the dates and the errors that you've pointed out, is the statement a fair and accurate reflection of your declaration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: The statement is correct, but as for the dates, I'm not 100 per cent sure about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And does the statement, aside from the dates and the errors that we spoke about, does it accurately reflect what you would say if you were to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: If you were to ask me the same thing today I would answer in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would ask that the statement be admitted pursuant to 92 ter at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? I hear none. So they are so admitted and then they will be marked subsequently or by the registrar and the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would also qualify that -- first, I guess I should clarify the record and say that it's designated P02288. And also, I would ask that the admission of the document into evidence be under seal at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed with the summary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness was born and raised in the village of Jaglici. At the age of 18, the witness served in the JNA under the national service programme for one year, and in April 1992, joined the Territorial Defence. In July 1995, after many people had left Jaglici for the UN-safe area - that's in quotes, page 2, paragraph 1, a UN-safe area - in Srebrenica, the witness remained in his village together with his wife and 13 month old daughter. The witness told his wife that they would only leave when he was no longer able to defend them. That day came on 11th July 1995. At around 8.00 p.m., the witness and other members of the Territorial Defence were ordered out of their trenches in order to meet and discuss what should be done in the face of news about the fall of Srebrenica. It was decided that women, children and the elderly should go to Potocari while the witness and other men were advised to gather in Susnjari. As a result, the witness separated from his wife and infant daughter. In Susnjari, at around 10.00 p.m., it was decided that a column would be formed in an attempt made to walk to the free territory. The column consisted of approximately 17.000 to 18.000 people including some women, children and elderly. That night, the column set out toward the free territory at around midnight. That part of the column which the witness was located -- in which the witness was located set out at approximately -- set out approximately two hours later owing to the size and length of the column. At about 8.00 a.m., on 12th July, the column encountered its first ambush near a stream at the base of the hill of Buljim. This ambush occurred about 500 metres behind the witness and killed approximately 30 people. The column however would be ambushed several more times. At about 9.30 p.m. near Kamenica, the column was shelled and came under fire while attempting to cross the asphalt road traversing Konjevic Polje and Kravica. The witness escaped this ambush climbing to higher ground and hiding behind a tree. However, between 500 and 1.000 people were killed. After regrouping and setting off carrying the wounded on make-shift stretchers, the witness came under direct fire as the column was again ambushed. The witness fell to the ground beneath wounded individuals on stretchers and those carrying them. They were all killed. Covered in blood, the witness waited until the shooting stopped and then got up. He found a gathering group from the column nearby and joined them. As this new group eventually began to move, they came under fire. And approximately 200 people died in this attack. At a certain point that night, the early morning of the 13th of July 1995, the witness recalled seeing other refugees engage in strange behaviour including suicides and shootings. Still the group proceeded. They decided to go towards Sandici in order to cross the asphalt road there. Near a clearing close to the road, another ambush ensued and another 200 people were killed. The witness escaped, running into the woods and sliding down a steep embankment. The group walked another three kilometres before making another attempt to cross the asphalt road. Somewhere near Sandici, the group again came under fire. At about 8.00 a.m., the witness could see Serb soldiers on the road running from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, there were APCs on the road, tanks and other military vehicles on the road. Serb soldiers were telling those, telling people who had not crossed the road to surrender. The soldiers told them they would not be harmed, that they would be bussed to Tuzla. They told them that if they did not surrender women and children in Potocari would be harmed. The witness saw about 200 civilians surrender. They were ordered to take off their shirts, which were placed in a pile by the soldiers. Though were lined up into rows and then they were shot down with automatic weapons and anti-aircraft machine-guns. Sometime thereafter, the witness managed to get across the asphalt road with his group some distance away. Lost in the hills, the group descended ending up at a point along the same road it had earlier crossed. There, the witness observed around 35 corpses lying on the roadside and smashed as if they had been run over by military vehicles. Soon thereafter, in the vicinity of Pervani, the municipality of Pervani, the group came under fire once again. Half the group decided to surrender while the witness and others fled. After walking for sometime, the group arrived at Konjevic Polje. Trying to cross the road, they soon found themselves in front of a school used by the Serbs as military barracks. The group was fired upon and many were killed. The witness and a few others escaped and eventually proceeded towards Kuslat. The group continued on trying to reach the free territory. They reached Kuslat. They crossed the Drinjaca River there and some people were washed away. They continued towards Snagovo. There, they came under fire trying to cross an asphalt road. They retreated until early the next morning. On the 16th of July, when they managed to get across, two people were killed in this effort, including the witness's neighbour. The group continued on to Baljkovica. There they joined about a thousand people from the column. While the majority of the group turned back towards Zepa because of the Serb lines, the witness together with 21 others, decided to try to get through. While at Baljkovica, the witness saw many black and bloated bodies, corpses. Attempting to cross the Serb lines, the group drew fire and had to wait. The next afternoon, either the 18th or the 19th of July at about 2 p.m. the witness awoke to the sounds of calls for surrender by nearby soldiers. From about 20 metres away, the group came under fire. The witness surrendered, as did five other people that he knew. That day, the witness lost track of his brother who was still in the bush when the witness surrendered. The witness would never see -- would never hear from him again. The witness observed that the soldiers wore uniforms bearing a badge which had the colours of the Serbian flag and above a spread eagle. Also written in Cyrillic were the words "Army of the Republika Srpska." It's a quote from page 5, paragraph 11. As the witness surrendered, he was struck by a rifle butt and knocked to the ground. He saw other people who he knew lying face down on the ground. The witness was questioned about his military status. During this time a soldier came up and asked permission to kill a prisoner with his bayonet. He was granted permission to choose one, upon which he chose the witness. The witness was then made to lie down next to the other captives. Soon thereafter, and within only a few metres of the witness, they were taken up and shot to death one by one. The witness was the last remaining when the soldiers were ordered not to kill him so that he could be used for prisoner exchange. The witness was transported to Zvornik by the military police whom he identified as having worn badges containing the three colours of the Serbian flag, together with the cross containing an S in Cyrillic in each quarter. And that's a quote from page 6, paragraph 12. In Zvornik the witness was detained with about 39 other prisoners in a paint and wood varnish factory where he was severely beaten and regularly interrogated. On the 21st July, 1995, the witness was loaded on to a truck as were half the other prisoners and taken to, "A concentration camp near Batkovic." Paragraph 6, paragraph 13. While there, the men were forced to work on farms and in factories. And finally five months later, on the 24th December, 1995, the witness was released. That concludes my summary. If I may put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, are you a Bosnian by nationality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please use your discretion if at any time we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, are you a Bosnian by nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court briefly whether you're presently employed? And without telling us where you are employed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what is it -- what it is that you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I'm a worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What kind of work do you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I work in construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long have you been doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Not for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us approximately how long you've been doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prior to that, did you hold any other employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, do you live alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you live with your wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what their ages are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: 12 and a half and nine and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long is it that you have been married?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And prior to your departure, prior to the time that you left Jaglici, were you active in the armed forces, in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for how long had you been active in the military prior to July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: From April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what it is your responsibilities were in the military during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you have any responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. I was going to let you finish this, and interrupt you later. But let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you feel the need to go into private session, please feel free to ask that and we will grant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to direct your attention, Mr. Witness, to the date that you were captured. That would have been around the 18th or the 19th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that day, can you tell us about or around the time of your capture, how that transpired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: We were exhausted and we fell asleep. Sometime in the afternoon, maybe around 1.00 or 2.00, we heard somebody calling to us, telling us to surrender because we were encircled and there was no exit for us. I lifted my head and looked around and I saw that there were Chetniks all around us. We were encircled and indeed there was no exit anywhere. They called us once to surrender. We kept quiet and then they opened fire but they did not aim at us. Then they called us another time, and asked us to surrender. We kept quiet. They opened fire again, this time they aimed in the air. And the third time they invited us to surrender. We kept quiet again, then they started shooting at us. And then when the shooting stopped and when they called out to us again, then some people stood up, started surrendering and coming out up to the road. I continued being quiet. I didn't want to get up. And then one of their commanders issued an order to them to comb the terrain, to throw grenades from hand-held rocket launchers. I knew that I would certainly die there and then I decided to stand up. I stood up. I started walking up there. I threw my rifle. I came to the road, and they asked me if I had something on me. I said I didn't have anything on me. And then they searched me again. They searched me thoroughly and as I was passing one, one was going to kick me in the stomach, I turned around, so he kicked me in the hip, and while I was passing, another one hit me with a rifle butt and cut my neck with it. As I descended, the five guys that surrendered before me were on their bellies on the ground and as I was approaching them they told me, "You can lie down together with them." I was the sixth in that row.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I stop you for a moment? Can I ask you first if you know approximately where this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I heard it on the radio when they mentioned the place called Tisova Kosa. There was mentioned on the radio. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this that location you believe you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe they referred to it as Baljkovica, but when they spoke about that place on the radio set, on Motorolas, they mentioned something as Tisova Kosa. People refer to that place as Baljkovica, when I came there. And this may have happened some two or three kilometres off the place that they referred to as Baljkovica. This is where I was captured, some two or three kilometres away from that. Since I'm not familiar with the ground, that was the first time I was there, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated also that you had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes, I did have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it is that you came into possession of the weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: I got it from a man who had been killed, and I came by his body on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, could we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are allowing it this time because it basically touches upon the -- some vital part of his testimony, but otherwise, please try to avoid repetitions which could be -- serve no other purpose except by way of repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do apologise. I intend to be as brief as possible with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated that the soldiers that you had observed had some emblems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes. There was the eagle with four letters S in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you observe any other insignia with respect to any other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: It was the same insignia, except that they were from the military police, the insignia was the same but on these other emblems, it said, "Military police" also in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have any indication through any conversation you had with any of the soldiers as to from where they came, what unit they were with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: The soldier with the bayonet in his hand asked me, "What do you think, where we are from?" I was confused and frightened. I don't know. I thought that they were from Serbia. I said, "I think that you are from Serbia." He said, "No, we are not." I was silent. I didn't want to ask him anything. He himself said that they were from the Krajina. "We are Krajisniks."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While you were -- during the course of your capture, were you questioned by any officers or other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: You mean when I was brought to Zvornik or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you were brought to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: An officer did come in. I don't know if his last name was Vukasinovic or Vukadinovic. I'm not sure. It's one or the other. He told me to confess everything I know, otherwise things would not go well for me. The second condition he said was that if I said everything the way it was, that my brother would be exchanged together with me, who remained behind when I was captured at that same place. I didn't know what happened with him. He also intended to surrender but they fired at him, actually, at the four of them, who had stayed behind there. And I simply didn't know what happened to them. Most probably they were killed there. I thought that he was still alive when this man came in and said what he said, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you questioned by any other officers or soldiers while you were in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: Yes. Soldiers were coming in, asking about this and that, all kinds of things, beating me, and I think the next morning I was interrogated. I think it was a security person, a person who worked in security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you describe the person that interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: He was overweight. He wasn't too tall. He had grey hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he identify -- well, what led you to the conclusion that he was a security officer or worked in security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139
utterances.text: What led me to that conclusion was that I was also interrogated at the camp in Batkovic, and when I was interrogated there, the soldiers who took me there, they would come and get me and they would say, "You're going to the security people for interrogation." And that's where this stuck in my mind, when I was interrogated in Zvornik, I wasn't 100 per cent sure that this man was a security person, but when I was in Batkovic and they said, "You're going to the security people for interrogation," then it came to me that probably the person who interrogated me before, over there, was also a security man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, time is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll leave it until tomorrow. We'll leave it until tomorrow. We don't like to keep the staff here unduly and also because there is another Trial Chamber sitting at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, we will see you again tomorrow afternoon when hopefully we will finish with your testimony. In the meantime, please, between now and then, you're not to communicate or let anyone communicate with you in relation to the matters that you are testifying about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we can leave. You can draw the curtains because there is members -- there are members of the public in the gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
